title: Two-source interference experiments and conditions
prior_knowledge_summary: Lesson 7 established interference, coherence and the path-difference conditions for constructive and destructive interference.
Lesson 6 established that diffraction spreads waves and makes overlap possible.
new_learning: Two-source demonstrations using water, sound, light and microwaves.
Source, overlap, contrast and detection conditions needed for a stable observable pattern.
not_yet_taught: recall and use λ = ax / D for double-slit interference using light

learning_outcomes.statement: Show an understanding of experiments that demonstrate two-source interference using water waves in a ripple tank, sound, light and microwaves.
Understand the conditions required if two-source interference fringes are to be observed.

evidence_basis.note: P2 evidence grounds two-source apparatus, path-difference interpretation, pattern observation and condition changes. No P1 lesson assignment inferred.

blocks.title: Why does a detector find loud and quiet places?
content: Two loudspeakers play the same steady tone. A microphone moves across the room. Its reading rises, falls, then rises again even though both speakers stay on. The puzzle is not a changing source. It is a changing path difference.
We will build the same idea with water, sound, light and microwaves, then ask what must stay controlled for the pattern to remain visible.

figure.purpose: Create the experimental puzzle and show that position changes two path lengths.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful teacher sketch of two loudspeakers and a microphone at three positions. Draw paired paths to each position and simple high-low-high meter readings. Do not label the interference answers.
figure.alt_text: A microphone moved across two speakers has changing path lengths and changing readings.

blocks.title: One engine, two sources, an overlap region

controlled_definitions.displayed_content: a constant phase difference between two waves

content: Coherence is a constant phase difference between two waves. For a stable pattern, the sources must be coherent and have the same frequency. Their waves must overlap. Comparable amplitudes give clear maxima and deep minima; very unequal amplitudes leave weak contrast because cancellation is incomplete.

It is tempting to say two sources are enough. That feels right because two waves can meet, but independent sources usually drift in relative phase. Then maxima and minima wander and average away. A single oscillator feeding both sources keeps their phase relationship fixed.

figure.purpose: Separate the source, overlap, coherence and contrast conditions.
figure.brief: Rectangular hand-drawn four-box condition map: one oscillator feeding two sources, overlapping wavefronts, fixed phase clock, and comparable amplitude bars. Use ticks beside stable conditions and no decorative scene.
figure.alt_text: A condition map shows coherent equal-frequency sources, overlap and comparable amplitudes.

blocks.title: Water and sound make the pattern easy to explore
content: In a ripple tank, attach two dippers to the same vibrator. Circular waves spread and overlap. Use a lamp or stroboscope to see alternating nodal lines and strong-motion regions. Moving along a line across the pattern changes the path difference from the dippers.

For sound, feed two loudspeakers from one signal generator. Move a microphone connected to a level meter through the overlap region. Loud positions are constructive; quiet positions are destructive. Reflections should be reduced because extra reflected paths can mask the two-source pattern.

figure.purpose: Compare how water displacement and sound intensity reveal the same interference structure.
figure.brief: Rectangular split teacher sketch. Left: same vibrator, two ripple-tank dippers and curved nodal lines. Right: one generator, two speakers and microphone track with alternating high and low readings. Label source, overlap and detector only.
figure.alt_text: Ripple-tank and loudspeaker demonstrations reveal alternating reinforcement and cancellation.

blocks.title: Light needs two narrow openings from one wavefront
content: For light, illuminate two narrow, close slits with one monochromatic source. Each slit diffracts the same incident wavefront, so the slits act as coherent secondary sources. Their overlapping light on a screen produces alternating bright and dark fringes.

Narrow slits help diffraction spread the light into the same region. Close spacing helps the overlap pattern be resolvable. Monochromatic light avoids many wavelengths placing bright and dark regions at different positions. This lesson describes the pattern only. The fringe-spacing equation comes next.

figure.purpose: Show why one illuminated pair of narrow slits supplies coherent overlapping light.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper sequence diagram: monochromatic source, single incident wavefront, two narrow slits, diffracted overlap and screen with alternating bright and dark bands. Do not include dimensions or fringe-spacing formula.
figure.alt_text: One monochromatic wavefront illuminates two narrow slits whose diffracted light overlaps on a screen.

blocks.title: Microwaves let us measure the path rule directly
content: Feed two microwave transmitters from the same source and move a detector through their overlap region. Record maxima and minima. At any detector position, subtract the two source-to-detector distances to find path difference.

This is the Lesson 7 formula to remember. Δx is path difference, λ is wavelength and n is an integer. For in-phase sources, whole wavelengths give maxima and odd half wavelengths give minima. Example: routes 0.84 m and 1.02 m differ by 0.18 m. With λ = 0.060 m, Δx/λ = 3.0, so the detector is at a maximum. Reversing the subtraction gives the same magnitude.

figure.purpose: Model a complete detector-position path-difference check.
figure.brief: Rectangular annotated microwave layout with two coherent transmitters, detector, routes 0.84 m and 1.02 m, and a side calculation 0.18/0.060=3.0 leading to a meter maximum. Keep geometry original.
figure.alt_text: Two microwave routes differ by three wavelengths, giving a detector maximum.

blocks.title: A pattern can exist but still be hard to observe
content: A dark fringe does not mean that each source sends no wave there. Both waves arrive, but equal opposite displacements cancel. If amplitudes differ, the minimum is not zero. If phase drifts, the dark position moves. If waves do not overlap or the detector cannot resolve the changes, no clear pattern is recorded.

Use this practical route: create two coherent same-frequency sources, make their waves overlap, keep amplitudes comparable, choose a detector suited to the wave, then move the detector or observe a screen. Explain each maximum or minimum using path difference and phase. Water, sound, light and microwaves change the apparatus, not the interference physics.

figure.purpose: Consolidate faults that reduce visibility without confusing them with absence of waves.
figure.brief: Rectangular diagnostic table with four rows: drifting phase, unequal amplitudes, no overlap, coarse detector. Show the observed consequence beside each and finish with a compact source-overlap-detect-explain flow.
figure.alt_text: A diagnostic table links failed conditions to moving, shallow, absent or unresolved fringes.

misconceptions_addressed: Any two independent sources give stable fringes.
A dark fringe means neither source sends a wave there.
Coherence alone guarantees a clear pattern even without overlap or adequate detection.
